description: Every rejection the registration transcript exists to produce. Except where a vector says otherwise, each one is the first accept vector with exactly one input substituted, so the field that changed is the field that caused the rejection. stage names the frozen check that refuses it. verifiesMathematically is what a lenient verifier gets: one that accepts either base64 alphabet with or without padding, takes DER or fixed-width r||s, and asks its ECDSA library whether the numbers work out over serverTranscript under the key inside the presented certificate request. A vector that is rejected while verifiesMathematically is true is a vector the library alone would have accepted, and is the reason the rule and not the library decides. null means there was no usable key to ask with.

vectors.name: protocol major version the exchange does not support
vectors.note: The bytes are the accepted exchange untouched. protocol/agent/v1/authentication.md already owns this rejection and it happens before anything here is parsed, which is why the proof still verifies.

vectors.name: malleated high-S proof over the accepted transcript
vectors.note: The pair (r, n - s) of the accepted proof. Every ECDSA library verifies it, so the encoding rule and not the library has to refuse it.

vectors.name: DER encoded proof
vectors.note: The same r and s in ASN.1. This surface has exactly one signature encoding.

vectors.name: padded base64url proof
vectors.note: The same 64 octets with = padding. Two spellings of one proof would make the proof useless as an exchange identity.

vectors.name: standard base64 alphabet proof
vectors.note: Unpadded, right length, wrong alphabet. Whether it is even distinguishable from base64url depends on the bytes, which is exactly why the alphabet is fixed rather than sniffed.

vectors.name: truncated proof
vectors.note: Sixty octets. Left-padding it back to 64 would change r, so a verifier rejects rather than repairs.

vectors.name: proof whose r and s are both zero
vectors.note: Well formed in length and alphabet, out of range in value.

vectors.name: proof declaring ES384
vectors.note: The value is the accepted proof. algorithm is a closed enumeration, so an unrecognised value is refused rather than ignored in favour of what the bytes look like.

vectors.name: proof declaring none
vectors.note: The JWS "none" downgrade, refused before any key is loaded.

vectors.name: certificate request carrying a P-384 key
vectors.note: A structurally valid, correctly self-signed PKCS#10 whose key is on the wrong curve. ADR 0008 fixes P-256 for the device identity and this surface may not widen it.

vectors.name: certificate request whose self-signature was altered
vectors.note: One octet of the PKCS#10 signature flipped. The structure parses and the key is intact, so only actually checking the self-signature catches it.

vectors.name: certificate request that is not DER at all
vectors.note: Arbitrary octets. They still have a SHA-256 and therefore still produce a transcript, which is why the certificate request is checked before the proof rather than after it.

vectors.name: replay of an accepted exchange against the token it already spent
vectors.note: Byte-identical to the accepted exchange, replayed after the token was consumed. The proof still verifies and must: replay is a state decision the token row owns, not a signature failure.

vectors.name: accepted exchange presented after its token expired
vectors.note: The same octets five minutes after expiresUnix. Freshness is evaluated against the Connect clock and the stored row; the proof itself never goes stale, which is why an expiry lives in the transcript and a window does not.

vectors.name: proof produced by a key other than the one in the certificate request
vectors.note: A real ES256 signature over the correct transcript, by the wrong key. The verifying key is only ever the one inside the presented certificate request.

vectors.name: accepted proof presented against a different token of the same cluster
vectors.note: The token uid, the challenge nonce, and the expiry all come from the other row, so the rebuilt transcript differs in three fields at once.

vectors.name: accepted proof presented against another cluster of the same organization
vectors.note: Only clusterUid differs. A device enrolled by an operator of one cluster can never land in another, even inside the tenant it belongs to.

vectors.name: accepted proof presented against a cluster of another organization
vectors.note: The cross-tenant case. organizationUid is in the transcript so that a proof is unusable outside the tenant that issued its token even if every other value were somehow reproduced.

vectors.name: accepted proof moved onto a different requestId
vectors.note: A captured body resubmitted under a fresh idempotency key. Binding requestId is what keeps a captured exchange replayable only as itself.

vectors.name: accepted proof against a row whose challenge nonce differs
vectors.note: Everything a console reader can see is unchanged; only the value delivered once with the secret differs. A proof cannot be precomputed from public token metadata.

vectors.name: accepted proof against a row whose expiry was extended
vectors.note: One hour added to expiresUnix. A window that is widened after the fact invalidates every proof produced for the old one instead of quietly resurrecting them.

vectors.name: accepted proof presented with a substituted certificate request
vectors.note: A perfectly valid, correctly self-signed certificate request for an attacker key. This is the vector that a verifier checking only the PKCS#10 self-signature would accept, and it would issue a device certificate for the attacker.

vectors.name: proof over a transcript whose expiry carries a leading zero
vectors.note: A real signature over a transcript whose sixth field reads 11:01787228100 instead of 10:1787228100. The length prefix moves with the value, so a variant spelling of one integer is a different transcript and not an equivalent one. A verifier normalising the number instead of refusing the proof would give one exchange two valid transcripts.

vectors.name: proof over a transcript separated by 0x00 instead of 0x0a
vectors.note: The separator ADR 0009 uses for a signed document, applied to a transcript that fixes 0x0a. Two separator conventions must not produce one accepted proof.

vectors.name: proof over a transcript whose domain is lowercased
vectors.note: The domain is compared as octets. Case folding it would let a producer pick either spelling and give one exchange two identities.

vectors.name: proof over a JSON serialisation of the same field values
vectors.note: The transcript is not a document and is never JSON. A JSON signature input would make key order, escaping, and number formatting part of the contract.
